title: Final Parking Space: 1987 Volvo 760 GLE Turbo Wagon with Nearly 400K Miles

body_markdown:
Those who fall in love with brick-shaped Volvos tend to keep their cars on the street for decades, after a cold-blooded look at resale value would suggest it’s time to get something from our current century, which means I still have no problem finding[interesting](https://www.murileemartin.com/Junkyard/JunkyardGallery-Volvo.html) Swedish[iron](https://www.murileemartin.com/Junkyard/JunkyardGallery-Saab.html) in junkyards. Today’s FPS subject is an exceptionally well-traveled 700-Series wagon that now resides in[a Denver-area car graveyard](https://www.upullandpay.com/locations/colorado/aurora/) .


Volvo


The entire family of angular rear-wheel-drive Volvos, affectionately known as “Swedish Bricks,” was born in 1966. That’s the year in which the first[Volvo 144](https://www.volvocars.com/intl/media/press-releases/B491DB776953818D/) rolled off the line in[Västra Götalands län](https://goteborg.se/) . In the above photo, you can see the Brick’s general design: unibody structure with solid rear axle and coil springs all around.


Volvo


The 140-Series wasn’t the first Volvo to ride on that chassis design, of course. That car borrowed a great deal from the underpinnings of its predecessor,[the Amazon](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/is-there-a-classic-more-practical-than-this-volvo-amazon/) (which was sold as the 122S in North America).


Bring a Trailer


But wait! The Amazon itself contained a great deal of chassis DNA from *its* predecessor, the[PV544/PV544](https://www.autoweek.com/car-life/classic-cars/a32607043/junkyard-treasure-1959-volvo-pv544-sport/) . This car has a design that dates back to 1944, making it one of the world’s only *midwar* civilian cars (there are advantages to being a carmaking nation that stayed neutral during World War II).


All that history means you can trace the Brick’s direct bloodline all the way back to 1944, and forward until the very last 900-Series[V90](https://www.autoblog.com/features/junkyard-gem-1997-volvo-v90/) s and[S90](https://www.autoblog.com/features/junkyard-gem-1998-volvo-s90/) s were sold as 1998 models. Today’s FPS car represents a critical chapter of that history: the one that the brains in Göteborg wrote when they needed a follow-up to the most iconic Swedish car of all time.


Volvo


That car was[the 200-Series](https://www.volvocars.com/us/media/models/200series/1974/) (itself a 144-Series with a MacPherson-strut front suspension and different bodywork from the A-pillar forward), which proved to be such a global sales hit that it stayed in production with only minor tweaks from 1974 through 1993. Today’s FPS car is just the second Volvo in the series, after[a 1985 DL sedan](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/final-parking-space/final-parking-space-1985-volvo-244-with-nearly-400k-miles/) (aka 244) that got even closer to the 400,000-mile final odometer figure. Sorry for the lack of FPS honorees here, Volvo fans, but I’ll get you a discarded PV544 or Amazon as soon as I can…


Volvo


The fascinating thing about the 700-Series Volvo is that its supposed predecessor stayed in production *after* it stopped being built. Plenty of 240 owners wanted new 240s when their old cars reached age 10 or 15, despite more modern models sitting next to them in the showrooms, and Volvo was happy to provide them.


Bring a Trailer/Robkeller


The 700-Series was based on the chassis design of the 200-Series and shared its powertrains, but its body and interior were entirely new. It was sold in the United States from the 1983 through 1992 model years, with sedan, coupe, and wagon bodies (the Bertone-styled[780 coupe](https://www.thetruthaboutcars.com/2020/10/junkyard-find-1989-volvo-780-turbo-bertone-coupe/) was available here just for the 1987–91 model years).


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


Worldwide, the 700-Series was powered by 2.0- and 2.3-liter straight-four-cylinder gasoline engines with either single or double overhead cams; diesel straight-fours of 2.3-liter displacement (made by Volvo); and diesel straight-sixes displacing 2.4 liters (made by Volkswagen); plus gasoline- and diesel-burning 2.8-liter[PRV V-6s](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/could-this-turbo-engine-have-saved-delorean/) .


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


This car was built with the B230FT turbocharged and intercooled 2.3 SOHC four-banger, rated at 160 horsepower and 187 pound-feet. This was serious power for its time, and it inspired one owner to spray-paint “SWED SLED” on the underside of the hood.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


A junkyard shopper had already yanked the turbocharger and exhaust manifold before I’d arrived.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


Volvo chose to call the 700-Series cars with turbocharged four-cylinder engines 760s rather than 740s, though the second digit in the model name once indicated the number of engine cylinders, according to Volvo’s system; this was because adding a turbocharger had the same effect as adding cylinders. BMW did the same sort of thing with the Euro-market[E23 745i](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/klockau-classics/early-80s-bmw-745i-one-sleek-shark/) , which had a 3.2-liter turbocharged engine but received a designation that implied that it had a 4.5-liter engine, according to BMW’s naming system.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


Just to confuse everybody, Volvo sold U.S.-market 760s that *did* have six cylinders under their hoods, often alongside other 760s with four cylinders. Here’s[a 1983 760 GLE sedan with the VW-built turbodiesel six](https://www.autoweek.com/car-life/classic-cars/a32874830/junkyard-treasure-1983-volvo-760-gle-turbodiesel-sedan/) , for example; the PRV-equipped sedans and wagons also got 760 badging. Also befuddling was the fact that Volvo sold 740 Turbos with the same engines as the 760 Turbos, indicating trim-level ranking.


Team Parcheezi Jones and the Raiders of the Lost Marque


That very engine ended up being pulled by a 24 Hours of Lemons team and swapped into…[a Porsche 924](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mlmg_Q0U_WE) !


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


This car has a four-speed automatic transmission, which became mandatory equipment on the 760 Turbo after 1987. A four-speed manual transmission was base equipment for the ’87 760 Turbo, but found few takers in the United States.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


The MSRP for this car was $27,765, or about $83,640 after inflation. That’s more than the Peugeot 505 Turbo wagon but less than[the Mercedes-Benz 300 TE](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/final-parking-space/final-parking-space-1988-mercedes-benz-300-te/) .


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


In the end, this car justified its hefty price tag by lasting for nearly 40 years and traveling 380,630 miles during that time.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


It isn’t the highest-mile junkyard Volvo I’ve documented, not by a long shot. That honor goes to[a 1990 240 DL sedan with well over 600,000 miles on the clock](https://www.autoweek.com/car-life/classic-cars/a41645618/volvo-beats-honda-for-all-time-junkyard-treasure-odometer-record/) . The best-traveled 700-Series Volvo I’ve found was[a 1990 740 Turbo wagon with 493,549 miles](https://www.thetruthaboutcars.com/2020/02/junkyard-find-1990-volvo-740-turbo-with-nearly-500000-miles/) , followed by[a 1988 740 GLE wagon that drove 403,348 miles](https://www.thetruthaboutcars.com/cars/down-on-the-junkyard/junkyard-find-1988-volvo-740-gle-with-403-348-miles-44506630) . Today’s car is #7 among Volvos and #46 overall in the[Murilee Martin Junkyard Odometer Standings](https://www.murileemartin.com/Junkyard/JunkyardGallery-300kMileCars.html) , as of the time of this writing.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


It appears that the mileage was at 332K in the spring of 2017.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


But then this old Swede was found parked in a reserved parking area in early 2026 and towed away. The registered owner couldn’t or wouldn’t pay the hefty fines needed to free it from its imprisonment, and it came to this place.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


A 240 with this kind of scary odometer number might have been rescued, but not a 740. So here it sits.


Keep them dogies rolling!


Forget the Audi 5000S Turbo and the BMW 528e. One of the most satisfying automobiles you could ever sit in.


Holds eight very large dogs, even when you stack six Volvos atop it.


Always ready to put in a good day’s work. It’s a wagon… until you need a sedan.
